text: who are the authors of Attention Is All You Need?
label: short
rationale: Well-known fact the model holds (8 authors, Vaswani et al.). Stage 1 answers correctly in one call. Stage 2 spends three calls on the same fact: analyze is trivial, generate repeats it, and review (which only sees the draft, not the question) may add an unneeded disclaimer or trim the author list under the 120-word cap. Expect identical correctness, roughly 3x latency and tokens, no quality gain. Check both against data/papers.json entry 1706.03762.

text: what year did the BERT paper come out?
label: short
rationale: One-word answer (2018). Both graphs should get it right. The interesting measurement is overhead: Stage 2 should cost about three times the tokens for a one-line fact, and the review node may rewrite a correct one-liner into a longer, more polite paragraph. This is the clearest case where the fixed workflow is not worth it.

rationale: Expansion of an acronym (Low-Rank Adaptation). Stage 1 may append a short explanation. text: Can you compare chain-of-thought prompting with Tree of Thoughts? When would I actually want to use one instead of the other?
label: long
rationale: Open comparison that invites drift into ReAct, Reflexion, self-consistency and benchmark numbers. Stage 1 likely produces a long essay with loose structure. Stage 2's analyze step should pin the comparison axes (single path vs search, cost, when lookahead matters) and review forces a sub-120-word answer, so expect a tighter but thinner reply that may drop concrete evidence such as the Game of 24 result (4% vs 74%). Quality judgement hinges on whether the student wanted depth or focus.

text: I'm trying to decide for my thesis between full fine-tuning and LoRA for adapting a 7B model. Can you explain the trade-offs?
label: long
rationale: Trade-off question with a personal decision context. Stage 1 tends to list many bullets, quote specific numbers from memory (parameter and memory savings, rank choices) and give generic advice. Stage 2 should keep the answer anchored to the student's decision because analyze restates the request, and review must flag numbers it cannot verify; the word cap forces prioritisation of the two or three decisive factors. Expect Stage 2 to be more decision-oriented and more hedged, Stage 1 to be more detailed but more likely to assert unverifiable figures.

text: What's the difference between a VAE and a GAN, and why did diffusion models kind of take over from both of them?
label: long
rationale: Three sub-questions in one, with the third (diffusion) outside the cached papers. Stage 1 will likely ramble through history and math for several paragraphs. Stage 2's analyze should split the question into parts; the 120-word review cap then probably squeezes or drops the diffusion part, so expect a focused but incomplete answer. Good test of whether the fixed word limit is right for this domain and of how the workflow handles multi-part questions.

text: For a question-answering system over my lab's internal documents, should I go with RAG or fine-tune the model on the documents? What are the trade-offs?
label: long
rationale: Classic trade-off (freshness, provenance, cost, hallucination) that drifts into implementation advice (vector databases, chunking) in a single call. Stage 2's analyze should list missing facts (corpus size, update frequency, budget) and generate may ask clarifying questions instead of answering; review keeps it polite and short. Expect Stage 2 to be more structured and more likely to ask the student for details, Stage 1 to give a longer unconditional recommendation.

text: How many citations does the Reflexion paper (arXiv 2303.11366) have on Semantic Scholar right now?
label: needs_data
rationale: A live count the model cannot know. Stage 1 will either invent a confident number or say it cannot browse. Stage 2's analyze should list 'current citation count from Semantic Scholar' as a required fact it lacks, and review's instruction to say so when a fact cannot be verified should make the final answer explicitly hedged. Neither graph gets the right number; the difference to look for is honesty versus confident invention. Motivates the Semantic Scholar tool in Stage 4.

text: how many authors are on the Llama 2 paper?
label: needs_data
rationale: The model knows the list is long but not the exact count; data/papers.json entry 2307.09288 lists 68 authors, which is the ground truth. Stage 1 is likely to guess a round number with confidence. Stage 2 should express uncertainty after review, since the fact cannot be verified from the draft alone. Expect both to be wrong on the number; record whether Stage 2 admits it. The cached paper lookup tool fixes this in Stage 4.

text: Is this a real paper? 'Gated Memory Compression for Long-Context Transformers', A. Vaswani and J. Devlin, arXiv:1908.10084, NeurIPS 2021. I want to cite it but can't find the PDF.
label: needs_data
rationale: Fabricated reference anchored to a real id: 1908.10084 is 'Sentence-BERT' (Reimers & Gurevych, 2019) in data/papers.json. Correct answer: the title/authors/venue do not match that id. Stage 1 cannot check the id; Stage 2's review node should at least flag the fact as unverifiable; Stage 4's get_paper resolves it.
